source_refs.note: PDF 220 (book p. 218): unit 7 introduction and the 7.1 definition of rectilinear motion

blocks.text: Kinematics is the branch of mechanics that describes the motion of objects without considering the causes of motion. In this unit, we will explore how objects move along a straight line by studying key physical quantities such as displacement, velocity, and acceleration. Through sketching and interpreting displacement-time and velocity-time graphs, we will develop a visual understanding of motion. The unit also introduces the use of rates of change to analyze how displacement, velocity, and acceleration vary over time. Using differentiation and integration with respect to time, we will solve simple problems related to motion. For situations involving constant acceleration, we will apply appropriate kinematic formulae to determine unknown quantities. Finally, the concepts learned will be applied to real-life situations, such as the motion of vehicles, free fall, vertical projectile motion, relative motion, and the creation of realistic movement in animation.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Kinematics answers the questions "where is it, how fast is it going, and is it speeding up or slowing down?". It does not ask why (that is the job of forces, which you meet in Physics). So this unit is pure description of motion, and the tools are the ones you already have from calculus:
1. Differentiation gives a rate of change. Velocity is the rate of change of displacement, and acceleration is the rate of change of velocity.
2. Integration goes back the other way: from acceleration to velocity, and from velocity to displacement.
3. Graphs show the same story as pictures: the slope of a graph is a rate of change, and the area under a velocity-time graph is a displacement.
The unit is built step by step: 7.1.1 and 7.1.2 separate scalars from vectors, 7.1.3 defines average and instantaneous velocity and acceleration, 7.1.4 and 7.1.5 read displacement-time and velocity-time graphs, 7.1.6 derives the constant-acceleration equations, and 7.1.7 applies them to bodies moving up or down under gravity.
The motion of a particle along a straight line is called rectilinear motion.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Two words in this definition need care.
Particle: an object whose size we ignore, so that it can be treated as a single point. A car on a long road or a stone falling from a roof can be treated as a particle, because only its position along the line matters.
Straight line: the particle moves only forwards or backwards along one fixed line, for example a car on a straight road, a lift going up and down, or a ball thrown vertically upwards.
To describe such motion we fix a point O on the line (the origin) and choose one direction along the line as positive. The position of the particle at time \(t\) is then a single signed number \(x(t)\), exactly like a point on a number line: \(x = 5\) means 5 units on the positive side of O, and \(x = -3\) means 3 units on the negative side.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Kinematics describes motion (position, velocity, acceleration) without asking what causes it.
2. Rectilinear motion is the motion of a particle along a straight line.
3. On a straight line, position is one signed number \(x(t)\) measured from a fixed origin O; the sign shows on which side of O the particle is.
4. Calculus is the main tool of the unit: differentiate to get rates of change, integrate to go back.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Thinking that "rectilinear" means "at constant speed". It only means "along a straight line"; the particle may speed up, slow down, stop or turn back on that line.
2. Forgetting to fix the origin and the positive direction before writing any number; without them a value such as \(x = -3\) has no meaning.
